annotation_assessments.evidence_scope: The human brain-library screen initially yielded a clone containing COX11 and RBM30 plasmids. The investigators subsequently retested the two prey proteins separately with full-length ACDP4 and negative-vector controls, supporting each positive interaction. RBM4B is an RNA-binding protein, but no verified more specific partner-class term captures this pair. The assay does not establish a physiological RNA-regulatory role for CNNM4.

Separate yeast two-hybrid retesting supports the COX11 pair, and coexpression modifies metal-induced toxicity in HEK293 cells. COX11 is a copper-delivery assembly factor, so protein-folding chaperone binding would misclassify the partner. The proposed direct metal handoff and native complex architecture were not demonstrated.

The exact donor identities and current same-term records support the inherited cellular location. Independent human CNNM4 expression, surface labeling and transport measurements establish activity at the plasma membrane. The target appearing among PAINT sources is legitimate experimental grounding, while the historical ancestral placement has not been reconstructed. The short alternative product is not covered by the full-length experiments.

The current HPA record reports plasma-membrane staining in A-431, U-251MG and U2OS cells, with an uncertain reliability rating and additional actin-filament staining. Independent sequence-verified human CNNM4 localization and surface-labeling experiments corroborate the membrane location; the HPA rating is not converted into a new actin-function claim.

SL-0039 maps the recorded plasma-membrane location. Human CNNM4 membrane topology, surface expression and cellular transport independently support this broad location; polarized epithelial basolateral localization is a context-specific refinement rather than a universal exclusion of other membrane regions.

Human CNNM4 mediates magnesium export and regulates TRPM7-dependent influx. Mouse Cnnm4 loss causes reduced serum magnesium and intestinal malabsorption. The mapped donor records include positive experimental magnesium-homeostasis annotations; their animal and cellular contexts are kept distinct from historical PAINT node placement.

The actual IPR045095 record maps to magnesium ion homeostasis. Direct human CNNM4 transport and mouse physiological evidence establish this role independently of the family mapping. Family membership alone is not used to assign a particular transport mechanism to every CNNM paralog.

The sodium-transporter assertion has positive experimental grounding, and human CNNM4 assays permit a more precise coupled classification. Sodium removal blocks magnesium efflux, sodium restoration restores it, and SBFI/Mag-fura2 measurements show sodium entry alongside magnesium loss. The reported approximately 2:1 cellular flux relationship is consistent with electroneutral exchange; it is not a purified single-cycle stoichiometry. Full-length human structures and surface-controlled mutagenesis strengthen target attribution. The original propagation source remains intact; this refinement does not assert an error in historical PAINT placement.

The broad inherited process remains correct: human CNNM4 supports magnesium movement across the plasma membrane, with mouse intestinal physiology providing complementary in vivo evidence. The already-present transmembrane-transport assertion supplies route specificity, so no additional process assertion is needed.

The exact mouse ortholog has basolateral localization records. The cited study also uses human CNNM4-FLAG in polarized MDCK cells and detects it with the basolateral Na/K-ATPase marker below ZO-1. Endogenous mouse intestinal and ameloblast localization corroborates this context; CNNM4 is not claimed to be exclusively basolateral in every cell.

ACDP4 expression altered copper-, manganese- and cobalt-induced cell toxicity, and COX11 coexpression enhanced these effects. The authors explicitly called for direct metal-accumulation measurements; viability alone does not identify a transported metal or flux direction. Later direct magnesium measurements support CNNM4 cation homeostasis, while the original broad assertion is retained as contextual evidence.

The original COX11/RBM30 study supports physical association through two-hybrid experiments but leaves native architecture and metal handoff unresolved. Independent human CNNM4 cryo-EM directly demonstrates an MgATP-bound tetramer, and TRPM7 coimmunoprecipitation establishes another assembly context. These observations support the broad complex term without treating the original pair as a resolved native complex.

The logical inference from sodium-transporter activity is independently supported by human CNNM4 SBFI sodium measurements coupled to magnesium efflux. Sodium entry is the counter-ion component of exchange, not merely a downstream consequence of TRPM7 regulation.

The inference from magnesium-transporter activity agrees with human cellular efflux, sodium-dependence experiments and full-length structural/mutational evidence. It refers to the transport performed by CNNM4; TRPM7-dependent influx is described separately as channel regulation.

CNNM4 coimmunoprecipitates with TRPM7, including endogenous proteins, and modest WT human CNNM4 reexpression restores TRPM7 whole-cell currents and magnesium uptake in CNNM3/4-deficient cells. Similar surface-channel levels and the SLC41A1 comparator distinguish this from generic magnesium lowering. Human CNNM4 S196P and CBS-deletion variants retain current rescue despite impaired efflux. This is performed channel regulation, not assignment of the TRPM7 pore or kinase activity to CNNM4. The new MF has no typed ancestor/descendant overlap with the seeded terms or ATP-binding addition.

Purified human CNNM4 residues 359–511 bind radiolabeled ATP in a magnesium-dependent filter-binding assay with a GST control; the reported affinity is 43.4 ± 8.9 µM. Full-length human CNNM4 also contains bound MgATP in the cryo-EM structure. This is measured recognition rather than an inference from a domain name, and it does not establish ATP hydrolysis. The 263-residue alternative product lacks the assayed CBS segment. ATP binding is nonredundant with the transport and channel-regulator MFs.
